overview: The Hausa states were a group of kingdoms and cities, not one empire with a single ruler. Kano offers unusually rich surviving walls, palace buildings, markets and manuscripts. This card uses named Kano evidence without treating it as a description of every Hausa household or town.

periods.title: Growing cities and kingdoms
periods.summary: Hausa states formed among the major centralized societies of the region; individual towns have different histories.

periods.title: Courts, commerce and Islamic scholarship
periods.summary: Kano and Katsina connected local political life with wider Muslim scholarly networks.

periods.title: Revolution and changing rulers
periods.summary: The 1804 Islamic revolution led to the Sokoto Caliphate. This political transition should not be confused with an end to Hausa society.

sections.title: Through the gate and into the market

items.text: Kano’s earthen defenses developed in stages. Nigeria’s heritage nomination describes earlier foundations, medieval building and a further extension in the 1500s. Surviving earthworks are evidence of repeated urban investment, not a wall built all at once.
Kano’s gates controlled passage through its walls. The nomination links gateways, palace and market as parts of the historical city.

Kurmi market was arranged in lanes specializing in different goods, including leatherwork, textiles, metalwork and spices. A shopper could head toward the right craft instead of searching one enormous jumble. The nomination also records the market’s continuing activity.

Rumfa, who ruled Kano from 1463 to 1499, is credited with the palace. The complex separates administration, family space and service areas. Its present layout records a living institution with a long building history, not a frozen fifteenth-century family photograph.

In the 1490s, the scholar Muhammad al-Maghili visited Kano and Katsina. He wrote advice for Kano’s ruler Muhammad Rumfa. Political power involved arguments about justice and obligations as well as armies and walls.

A manuscript of one of those works survives in Morocco’s national library. Its preservation there shows that the written connections of Hausa courts reached beyond today’s national borders. A surviving copy is not necessarily the author’s own handwriting.

“تاج الدين فيما يجب على الملوك” is an Arabic title catalogued by Kano Archives: “The crown of religion concerning what is required of kings.” It belongs to the advice-to-rulers tradition associated with al-Maghili and Rumfa. The archive’s copy is not precisely dated here.

Language and script are different things. Kano’s archive preserves Arabic histories alongside the Hausa Song of Bagauda in Ajami, meaning Hausa written with adapted Arabic letters. A page in Arabic-looking script is not automatically in the Arabic language.

The archive’s digitization account describes locating manuscripts with community librarians and copyists, then photographing them on site. Preservation depends on families and local scholars as well as large institutions.

Hausa identity developed through language, social relationships, migration and intermarriage. The scholarly summary on Hausaness specifically includes people of Fulani, Arab, Tuareg and Nupe backgrounds. A colored political area cannot contain all the ways people identified themselves.

The political change beginning in 1804 created Sokoto’s emirates in much of Hausaland. It did not empty markets or make Hausa speech vanish. The atlas’s 1815 boundary marks a mapping transition, rather than the date every Hausa kingdom ended.
Kano’s continuing market and preserved manuscripts show continuity. Altered buildings and recopied texts still require careful dating.

ending.text: The Sokoto revolution beginning in 1804 changed rulership across much of Hausaland. Hausa communities and language continued through emirate and later colonial rule. There is no single extinction date for a people or uniform fall date for all these states.
